title: Judges 5:12–23
context: Judges 5:12–23 calls Deborah and Barak to rise and then reviews the tribes. Ephraim, Benjamin, Machir, Zebulun, Issachar and Naphtali came. Reuben deliberated at its sheepfolds, Gilead stayed beyond the Jordan, and Dan and Asher stayed by the sea. The battle at Taanach by the waters of Megiddo is told poetically: the stars fought from the sky and the river Kishon swept the enemy away. Meroz is cursed for failing to come to help the LORD. Several lines are textually and lexically difficult. Both traditions read the stanza as praise for willing participation and a rebuke of those who held back, with the victory credited to the LORD.

verses.text: ‘Awake, awake, Deborah! Awake, awake, utter a song! Arise, Barak, and lead away your captives, you son of Abinoam.’
verses.arminianNotes: Deborah is called to wake and sing, and Barak to rise and lead away his captives. Arminian readers see the call to action as both leaders stepping into what God had appointed, with Deborah’s song and Barak’s command working together.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and read the summons as a call to take up the victory God has given. Both traditions see the doubled "awake" as poetic urgency and note the partnership of Deborah and Barak described in chapter 4.

verses.text: “Then a remnant of the nobles and the people came down. The LORD came down for me against the mighty.
verses.arminianNotes: A remnant of nobles and people came down, and the LORD came down for Deborah against the mighty. Arminians see a small and willing group joining the LORD in battle, with God’s help making up for their weakness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and stress the phrase about the LORD coming down, which credits the victory to him. The Hebrew of the verse is difficult and translations differ. Both traditions see the LORD fighting on behalf of a remnant.

verses.text: Those whose root is in Amalek came out of Ephraim, after you, Benjamin, among your peoples. Governors come down out of Machir. Those who handle the marshal’s staff came out of Zebulun.
verses.arminianNotes: Ephraim, Benjamin, Machir and Zebulun responded. Arminian readers note the honor given to tribes that answered the call, and they read Machir as a clan of Manasseh (Numbers 32:39–40) whose leaders came down.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree. The phrase "whose root is in Amalek" is obscure and is often linked with Ephraimite territory associated with the name (compare Judges 12:15). Both traditions avoid building theology on uncertain details and read the verse as a roll of honor.

verses.text: The princes of Issachar were with Deborah. As was Issachar, so was Barak. They rushed into the valley at his feet. By the watercourses of Reuben, there were great resolves of heart.
verses.arminianNotes: The princes of Issachar were with Deborah and rushed into the valley with Barak, but Reuben was full of great resolves of heart. Arminian readers see the contrast between those who acted and those who only resolved, a warning that good intentions are not the same as obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and observe the gentle irony in Reuben’s "great resolves" that came to nothing. Both traditions read the verse as praising Issachar’s action and exposing Reuben’s hesitation, without speculating about Reuben’s reasons beyond what the song says.

verses.text: Why did you sit among the sheepfolds? To hear the whistling for the flocks? At the watercourses of Reuben, there were great searchings of heart.
verses.arminianNotes: Reuben is asked why it sat among the sheepfolds listening to the shepherds’ whistling, with great searchings of heart. Arminians see the rebuke falling on those who preferred comfort and livelihood to the shared struggle of God’s people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and note that the song repeats the line about Reuben’s heart, changing resolves to searchings, which deepens the irony. Both traditions apply the verse as a warning against indecision when God’s people are called to act together.

verses.text: Gilead lived beyond the Jordan. Why did Dan remain in ships? Asher sat still at the haven of the sea, and lived by his creeks.
verses.arminianNotes: Gilead stayed beyond the Jordan, Dan stayed with its ships, and Asher sat by the coast. Arminian readers see different excuses for holding back, each tribe protecting its own interests rather than joining the common cause.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that the song names these tribes without describing any punishment, unlike Meroz in 5:23. Judah and Simeon are not mentioned at all, and interpreters explain that silence in different ways. Both traditions read the verse as a rebuke of self-interest.

verses.text: Zebulun was a people that jeopardized their lives to the death; Naphtali also, on the high places of the field.
verses.arminianNotes: Zebulun and Naphtali risked their lives to the death on the heights of the field. Arminians see the highest honor given to those who risked everything, matching their role in the prose account (Judges 4:6, 10).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and read the verse as the climax of the tribal review. Both traditions see the song honoring costly faithfulness, and both note that Hebrews 11:32–34 includes Barak among those who acted by faith.

verses.text: “The kings came and fought, then the kings of Canaan fought at Taanach by the waters of Megiddo. They took no plunder of silver.
verses.arminianNotes: The kings of Canaan fought at Taanach by the waters of Megiddo but took no plunder of silver. Arminian readers note the irony that the enemy came for spoil and went home with nothing, which sets up the scene with Sisera’s mother in 5:28–30.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and observe the geography of the Jezreel valley where the battle took place. Both traditions read the verse as stressing the complete failure of a powerful coalition against the LORD and his people.

verses.text: From the sky the stars fought. From their courses, they fought against Sisera.
verses.arminianNotes: The stars fought from the sky against Sisera. Arminians read the line as poetic language for heaven itself joining the battle, so that creation fights on the side of the LORD’s people, without needing a literal account of the stars.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree that the image is poetic. Many connect it with the storm and flood that disabled Sisera’s chariots (compare 4:15 and 5:21). Both traditions read the verse as declaring that the battle was won by God’s power working through creation.

verses.text: The river Kishon swept them away, that ancient river, the river Kishon. My soul, march on with strength.
verses.arminianNotes: The ancient river Kishon swept the enemy away, and Deborah tells her soul to march on in strength. Arminian readers see God using a flood to defeat the chariots, and they read the closing line as Deborah encouraging herself to press on in faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that Sisera’s chariots, his military advantage (4:3), become useless in the flooded valley. Both traditions see God turning the enemy’s strength into weakness, and they read the final line as personal resolve rooted in the LORD’s help.

verses.text: Then the horse hoofs stamped because of the prancing, the prancing of their strong ones.
verses.arminianNotes: The horses’ hoofs stamped with the galloping of the strong ones. Arminians read the line as a vivid picture of the enemy cavalry in chaotic flight, the sound of a powerful army breaking up before God’s judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed interpreters agree and observe that the repeated sounds in the Hebrew imitate galloping. Both traditions read the verse as poetic description of the rout, and they agree that no doctrine hangs on the details of the image.

verses.text: ‘Curse Meroz,’ said the LORD’s angel. ‘Curse bitterly its inhabitants, because they didn’t come to help the LORD, to help the LORD against the mighty.’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD’s angel calls for a curse on Meroz because its people did not come to help the LORD against the mighty. Arminian readers see a sober warning that refusing to act when God calls is treated as a serious failure with real consequences.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and note that the LORD does not need help, yet he counts his people’s participation as helping him. Meroz is otherwise unknown. Both traditions read the curse as covenant judgment on those who stood aside, not as a general license to curse others.
